subject: Huawei pulled its next AI chip in by nine months
bodyMarkdown:
Huawei moved the launch of its next AI accelerator forward by nine months yesterday, and it gave a date and a roadmap to go with it. If you hold Nvidia through a pension or an index fund, which most working Canadians do without thinking about it, that schedule is the number worth writing down.

## What Huawei showed in Shanghai

Digitimes reported Thursday that Huawei opened its Connect conference in Shanghai by launching the Ascend 960 **supernode**, a cluster of chips wired together to behave like one machine, in this case 4,096 accelerator cards. The Global Times carried Huawei's numbers for it: 8 exaflops of FP8 compute and one petabyte of memory, which the company says is enough to train models with up to 10 trillion parameters. A single 960DT card is rated at 2 petaflops FP8 with 288 GB of memory. The timing is the actual news. Tom's Hardware reported that the 960DT now arrives in the first quarter of 2027, three quarters ahead of the schedule Huawei published last year, with a second version following in the third quarter.

## Why the fight moved to optics

The headline engineering change is optical. Huawei says it replaced 48,000 of the usual 800G optical modules with 5,500 near-package ones, cutting more than 550 kilowatts of draw per cluster and lifting availability to 99.8%. Think about why a company would spend its best engineers there. Export controls on lithography leave SMIC, the foundry that makes these chips, stuck near a 5 nm equivalent process for years yet, so Huawei cannot win on transistor density and has stopped pretending it will. It is competing on the parts Washington does not control: interconnect, packaging, optics and power. Keeping a rival off the best chip does not keep it from building a large machine. It makes the machine hotter, bigger and more expensive, and Chinese electricity is cheap.

## What still holds them back

**HBM**, the stacked memory that sits next to an AI chip and feeds it data fast enough to matter, is the choke point. SemiAnalysis has reported that SMIC can produce die for more than a million Ascend chips a year while domestic memory supply holds real output under 300,000 without stockpiled foreign HBM. Quartz reported that Xu Zhijun, Huawei's rotating chairman, said the company does not have enough capacity to satisfy demand in China alone, so it has no plan for a full international push. Nvidia, meanwhile, ships its Vera Rubin NVL144 rack this half at a claimed 3.6 exaflops of FP4 across 144 GPUs. Huawei will not take global share next year. Inside China, on Beijing's timetable, it can take a great deal.

## The takeaway

Watch the memory, not the benchmark slides. Whether Huawei's in-house HBM arrives on time decides how many of these racks get built, and that is the number I would track between now and Q1 2027. Watch the power figure too, because 550 kilowatts saved per cluster is the kind of result that moves where data centres get sited, and Canada has been pitching itself as the place with spare electricity and cold air. If the 960DT actually ships in Q1 2027, the case that export controls bought the United States a decade gets much harder to argue.
